title: Mara and the Compass
premise: In 1914 Cornwall, Coral Villalobos drives for suffragist Edith Marchmont and quietly reads the letters she delivers — a habit that has taught her every secret in the village. When a frightened child named Mara is left at their door with a note instructing them to forget her face, Coral recognizes the handwriting of Herr Aldous Brandt, a German clockmaker who once saved Edith's life and to whom Coral owes an unspoken debt of her own. As war is declared and anti-German fury sweeps the coast, Coral hides Mara, breaks the law to contact Brandt's imprisoned kin, and discovers the child is the daughter Brandt smuggled out of danger — proof of a promise made in peacetime. The novel ends with Coral escorting Mara through occupied waters to neutral Holland, choosing found family over safety, and returning home changed: no longer invisible, but the keeper of a memory everyone else was told to forget.
about_author: Paloma Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in coastal county records offices. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Letters I Wasn't Meant to Read
chapters.summary: Coral Villalobos, POV. Establishes her double life as driver and secret reader of letters in 1914 Cornwall, her careful invisibility, and her quiet devotion to her employer, suffragist Edith Marchmont. Emotional beat: the comfort and loneliness of knowing everything and belonging nowhere.

chapters.title: A Knock After Midnight
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. A child appears at the door during a storm with a note reading 'forget this face,' signed only with a clockmaker's mark Coral half-recognizes. Edith is away; Coral must decide alone whether to open the door wider or shut it. Emotional beat: fear cracking into reluctant tenderness.

chapters.title: Mara
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. The girl won't speak her surname but hums a German lullaby and repairs Coral's broken watch with uncanny skill. Coral realizes whose daughter she might be. Emotional beat: recognition dawning like cold water; the first fragile bond forms over mended gears.

chapters.title: What Aldous Brandt Owed
chapters.summary: Coral, POV, with flashback. Years earlier, clockmaker Aldous Brandt sheltered Coral when she fled her father's house; his kindness bought her silence and her loyalty. Now he is declared enemy, interned, and unreachable. Emotional beat: gratitude curdling into dread as peacetime debts come due in wartime.

chapters.title: Edith Returns
chapters.summary: Edith Marchmont, POV. Edith comes home from London mid-campaign, finds a child in her house, and must weigh her public reputation against a private promise. She and Coral clash over risk. Emotional beat: two women testing how much truth they can afford each other.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. War fever arrives: shop windows smashed, a German baker driven out, neighbors watching the Marchmont house. Coral invents a cover story — Mara is a niece from Bristol. Emotional beat: the claustrophobia of a small town becoming a surveillance state of gossip.

chapters.title: Reading the Enemy's Mail
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Delivering letters for the parish, she intercepts correspondence about interned Germans and learns Brandt is held on the Isle of Man — and that authorities are searching for a missing child. Emotional beat: guilt sharpening into purpose; her secret habit becomes a weapon.

chapters.title: The Clockmaker's Letter
chapters.summary: Mara, POV (first time). Through the child's eyes we learn fragments of the escape from London, the mother who didn't make it, and the instruction to trust 'the lady who reads letters.' Emotional beat: grief rendered small and practical, the way children carry it.

chapters.title: An Offer from Sergeant Quill
chapters.summary: Sergeant Quill, POV. The local policeman, not unkind but dutiful, suspects the Marchmont household and offers Coral a chance to confess before someone else reports them. Emotional beat: the seduction of surrender — how easy it would be to stop being brave.

chapters.title: Smugglers' Lane
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Following a lead from her letter-reading, Coral contacts a retired smuggler, Mrs. Tregose, about moving Mara by boat. The price is steep and the route dangerous. Emotional beat: hope arriving wrapped in menace; Coral commits to the plan she can't yet finish.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Edith, POV. Authorities search the house while Coral hides Mara in the cellar among Edith's confiscated suffrage papers. Edith stalls with magnificent fury, weaponizing her respectability. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into defiance; the women realize they are fighting the same old war.

chapters.title: What the Watch Knew
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Inside Brandt's repaired watch Coral finds a hidden message: coordinates, a name in Holland, and the words 'keep my promise.' She finally understands Mara was meant to reach him — or what remains of his family. Emotional beat: revelation and resolve fused; no turning back now.

chapters.title: Quill Closes In
chapters.summary: Sergeant Quill, POV. Quill traces the smuggler connection and confronts Coral privately, torn between duty and his own buried decency. He gives her until the tide turns Thursday. Emotional beat: mercy with a deadline; the antagonist revealed as a man, not a monster.

chapters.title: Thursday Comes Early
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. A neighbor denounces the household; Quill must act tonight. Coral wakes Mara, packs in minutes, and Edith chooses to stay behind as decoy, insisting her name will protect them both. Emotional beat: farewell without goodbye; love expressed as logistics.

chapters.title: The Long Road to Falmouth
chapters.summary: Coral and Mara, alternating POV. A night journey by cart, hedge, and rail, nearly caught twice — once by soldiers, once by Mara's own exhaustion and grief breaking open. Emotional beat: the child finally cries and lets Coral hold her; found family crystallizes under pressure.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tregose's Boat
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. At a black cove, the smuggler demands more money than exists; Coral trades the one thing of value she owns — Edith's car — and her own place on the boat if needed. Emotional beat: sacrifice made concrete; Coral learns what she's worth by what she'll give up.

chapters.title: Enemy Waters
chapters.summary: Coral and Mara, POV shared. The crossing: patrol boats, fog, engine trouble, and Mara steering by the stars her father taught her. Emotional beat: terror and wonder braided together; the sea as both threat and passage toward belonging.

chapters.title: Holland, Grey and Quiet
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. They land near Flushing and find the address: Brandt's sister, who reveals Aldous died in internment months ago — but left instructions and funds for whoever brought Mara. Emotional beat: grief arriving after the finish line; the promise kept to a man who never knew.

chapters.title: The Face Worth Remembering
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara refuses to let Coral leave as instructed; she gives Coral the repaired watch back and asks her to stay until she sleeps. Coral confronts the note's command — forget this face — and chooses disobedience. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh; memory as an act of love.

chapters.title: Return Passage
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. The journey home, uncertain whether Edith was arrested, whether Quill waited. Coral carries a letter from Brandt's sister testifying to everything. Emotional beat: anxiety tempered by transformation — the invisible woman now walks visibly, carrying proof.

chapters.title: The Trial of Edith Marchmont
chapters.summary: Coral, POV, courtroom climax. Coral takes the stand uninvited, reads Brandt's letter aloud, and shames the court with the truth of the promise kept. Quill corroborates. Edith is released; charges dissolve. Emotional beat: catharsis — private loyalty detonating public injustice.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: Coral, POV, epilogue, 1919. Peace returns; Mara's aunt visits with news the girl is thriving; Edith and Coral keep the house together, having become each other's family. Coral still reads letters — but now some are addressed to her. Emotional beat: belonging earned, memory kept, quiet joy.
